(CNN)  -- Despite acknowledgment from the White House a day earlier that a peace deal between Israel and the Palestinians is unlikely before a new U.S. president takes office, Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice said Friday she is confident that ongoing efforts would produce success. Israeli Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni, right, and U.S.  Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice speak Thursday. "Carried to its state of conclusion, it will produce a state of Palestine," Rice, referring to negotiations in the wake of last year's U.S. summit on Israel-Palestinian peace in Annapolis, Maryland, said at a joint news conference with Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas in Ramallah, West Bank. Rice is on her eighth trip to the region since the Annapolis summit. On Thursday, White House spokeswoman Dana Perino said the Bush administration does not "think that it's likely that it (a peace agreement) would happen before the end of the year." Rice said Friday that she realizes the lack of a peace agreement in the months following the Annapolis summit had caused some concerns that talks had stalled or might fail, but "it's quite the opposite -- the Annapolis process has laid the foundation for the eventual establishment for the state of Palestine." The purpose of her current trip, Rice said, was "to advance the Annapolis process," and while she did not speculate on a timetable for the future of the process or offer specifics on peace talks, she added, "I've seen them move forward a great deal in the past year." Both Israeli and Palestinian officials have expressed doubts about achieving a peace agreement before President Bush leaves office, but until this week U.S. officials had been more optimistic in their public comments. Speaking in Israel on Thursday, Rice blamed part of the inability to secure a deal on recent political changes in Israel, which she noted is "in the midst of elections." With Abbas on Friday, she emphasized that the commitment expressed by Abbas and Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert when they signed an agreement to work toward a peace deal by the end of 2008 is still strong. "I hope that the tremendous commitment (by both sides) is fully understood," Rice said. While Rice did not discuss any impact a new administration in Washington might have on the process, she said, "The United States really does understand why the Palestinian people want unity." Israel in recent months has seen political upheaval. Olmert resigned in September amid allegations of corruption. Kadima Party leader and Israeli Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni gave up efforts to form a new coalition government late last month and is seeking to hold early general elections, which could be held in February, Livni's spokesman has said. Olmert will continue to lead as Israel's interim prime minister until a successor assumes power either by forming a coalition in the current Knesset or through general elections. However, it is unclear whether he will be able to strike a deal with the Palestinians before Israel forms its new government. Last month, Rice postponed a trip to a Middle East conference because of the global crisis in financial markets.

Israeli Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni and U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice spoke Thursday.

Rice said Friday that she understands why the absence of an agreement in the months after Annapolis has led some to worry that the talks have lost momentum or could collapse. But she argued that the reality is different, saying the Annapolis effort has created the groundwork for the eventual creation of a Palestinian state.

Rice said the goal of her latest visit was “to advance the Annapolis process.” Although she avoided predicting when the effort might conclude and did not provide details about the negotiations, she said she had seen “a great deal” of progress over the past year.

Officials on both the Israeli and Palestinian sides have voiced skepticism that a deal can be completed before President Bush leaves office. Until this week, however, U.S. officials had sounded more hopeful in their public statements.

While speaking in Israel on Thursday, Rice attributed some of the difficulty in reaching an agreement to recent political developments in Israel, noting that the country is currently “in the midst of elections.”

Appearing with Abbas on Friday, Rice stressed that the pledge made by Abbas and Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert—when they agreed to work toward a peace accord by the end of 2008—remains firm. “I hope that the tremendous commitment” by both sides is fully understood, she said.

Rice did not address how a new U.S. administration might affect the peace effort, but she added that “the United States really does understand why the Palestinian people want unity.”

Israel has experienced significant political turmoil in recent months. Olmert stepped down in September after corruption allegations emerged. Late last month, Kadima Party leader and Israeli Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni abandoned her attempt to put together a new coalition government and began seeking early general elections, which her spokesman has said could take place in February.

Olmert will remain Israel’s interim prime minister until a replacement takes office, either by forming a coalition in the current Knesset or through nationwide elections. It remains uncertain, however, whether he can reach an agreement with the Palestinians before Israel establishes its next government.

**Rice says Palestinian state still possible despite doubts over timeline**

**RAMALLAH, West Bank (CNN)** — U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice said Monday she remains confident that the U.S.-backed Annapolis peace process will eventually lead to the creation of a Palestinian state, even as the White House has expressed doubts that Israelis and Palestinians can reach a final agreement before President Bush leaves office.

Speaking after talks with Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas in Ramallah, Rice said the negotiations launched at last year’s Annapolis conference remain the best path toward a two-state solution.

“I continue to believe that this process can and will lead to the establishment of a Palestinian state,” Rice said, emphasizing that both sides must keep working despite the obstacles.

The Annapolis conference, hosted by the Bush administration in Maryland, relaunched formal Israeli-Palestinian negotiations with the goal of reaching an agreement by the end of 2008. But progress has been slow, with disputes continuing over core issues including borders, Jerusalem, refugees and Israeli settlements.

Rice’s remarks came after White House officials recently acknowledged that a peace deal before Bush leaves office in January appears increasingly unlikely. The administration had made Israeli-Palestinian peace a major foreign policy goal in its final year, but officials have tempered expectations as negotiations have stalled.

Palestinian leaders have expressed frustration over continued Israeli settlement activity in the West Bank, saying it undermines confidence in the talks and threatens the viability of a future state. Israel has said security concerns and political realities complicate the process, while maintaining that negotiations with Abbas’ government should continue.

Rice said the United States would keep pressing both parties to honor their commitments and make progress where possible.

“The important thing is that the parties remain engaged and that the vision of two states — Israel and Palestine living side by side in peace and security — remains alive,” she said.

Her visit to Ramallah was part of a regional diplomatic push aimed at sustaining negotiations and preventing the Annapolis framework from collapsing before the end of the Bush administration.

**Rice Presses Ahead on Israeli-Palestinian Talks Amid Israeli Political Turmoil**

**RAMALLAH/JERUSALEM —** U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice used her latest Middle East trip to reaffirm Washington’s commitment to Israeli-Palestinian peace negotiations, even as the process remained under strain from continued disputes over settlements, security, borders and the growing political uncertainty surrounding Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert.

Rice met with Palestinian Authority President **Mahmoud Abbas** in Ramallah as part of a renewed diplomatic push following the U.S.-sponsored Annapolis process, which had set the goal of reaching a framework peace agreement between Israel and the Palestinians. Speaking after the meeting, Rice emphasized that the United States still viewed a negotiated two-state solution as achievable, but acknowledged that the talks faced serious obstacles and that both sides would need to make difficult decisions.

Rice said the negotiations were intended to address the core issues at the heart of the conflict: the borders of a future Palestinian state, the status of Jerusalem, Israeli security concerns, Palestinian refugees, settlements and the future of Israeli military presence in parts of the West Bank. She stressed that Washington was not seeking a superficial declaration, but rather meaningful progress toward an agreement that could lead to the creation of a viable Palestinian state living alongside Israel in peace and security.

### Meeting With Mahmoud Abbas

In her talks with Abbas, Rice discussed the status of negotiations between Israeli and Palestinian teams, as well as the situation on the ground in the West Bank and Gaza. Abbas pressed the United States to do more to halt Israeli settlement activity, remove roadblocks and ease restrictions on Palestinian movement, arguing that such measures were essential to preserving public confidence in the peace process.

Palestinian officials have repeatedly complained that negotiations cannot succeed while Israel continues settlement construction in the West Bank and East Jerusalem. They also argue that checkpoints, military incursions and economic restrictions undermine the authority of Abbas and the Palestinian Authority, particularly as it competes politically with Hamas, which controls the Gaza Strip.

Rice acknowledged Palestinian concerns and said the United States opposed actions that prejudge the outcome of final-status talks. She reiterated that Israeli settlement expansion was not helpful to the peace process and that both sides had obligations under the U.S.-backed “road map” peace plan. For Israel, that includes a freeze on settlement activity; for the Palestinians, it includes continued efforts to improve security and prevent attacks against Israelis.

At the same time, Rice praised Abbas as a negotiating partner committed to diplomacy and nonviolence. She said strengthening Palestinian institutions remained a central part of U.S. strategy, including support for security forces loyal to the Palestinian Authority and efforts to improve economic conditions in the West Bank.

### Peace Negotiations Under Pressure

The Israeli-Palestinian negotiations were launched with considerable fanfare at the Annapolis conference, but progress has been difficult to measure publicly. Israeli and Palestinian negotiators have held repeated rounds of talks, but both sides have avoided revealing details, citing the sensitivity of the issues.

U.S. officials have continued to say that the goal is to reach an agreement before the end of President George W. Bush’s term. Rice, one of the administration’s most active advocates of the peace process, has made frequent trips to the region to keep pressure on both sides.

However, the talks remain constrained by political realities. Abbas leads the Palestinian Authority in the West Bank, but his authority does not extend to Gaza, where Hamas seized control in 2007 after violent clashes with Fatah. Israel and the United States consider Hamas a terrorist organization and have refused to negotiate with it unless it recognizes Israel, renounces violence and accepts previous agreements.

On the Israeli side, Olmert has supported continued negotiations with Abbas and has spoken publicly about the need for a two-state solution. But his government has faced criticism from both the right and the left. Right-wing parties oppose major territorial concessions in the West Bank or any division of Jerusalem, while left-leaning critics argue that settlement construction and military policies are undermining the peace effort.

Rice sought to keep the diplomatic track alive despite these complications. She indicated that the United States would continue working with both parties and said that even partial progress could be significant if it clarified the contours of a final agreement.

### Israeli Political Turmoil: Olmert Under Pressure

Rice’s visit came at a time of mounting political turmoil in Israel. Prime Minister **Ehud Olmert** was under intense pressure due to corruption investigations, including allegations involving improper financial contributions and other misconduct. Although Olmert denied wrongdoing, the investigations weakened his authority and raised doubts about whether he could deliver on any peace commitments.

The uncertainty surrounding Olmert’s political future cast a shadow over the negotiations. Palestinian officials questioned whether an Israeli prime minister facing possible resignation or political collapse had the mandate to make historic concessions. Israeli officials, meanwhile, insisted that negotiations could continue regardless of domestic political developments.

Olmert’s Kadima party began preparing for the possibility of a leadership contest, with Foreign Minister **Tzipi Livni** emerging as a leading candidate to succeed him. Livni, who served as Israel’s chief negotiator with the Palestinians, was seen internationally as a key figure in the peace process. She supported continued talks with Abbas and had built working relationships with U.S. and Palestinian officials.

However, Livni also faced a complex political landscape. If she were to replace Olmert as Kadima leader, she would need either to form a new coalition government or face early national elections. Coalition partners could demand policy concessions, and opposition parties could use the moment to push for a vote. That uncertainty made it unclear whether the peace process would accelerate, stall or be reshaped under new Israeli leadership.

### Livni’s Role and the Future of the Talks

Tzipi Livni’s prominence added another dimension to Rice’s diplomacy. As foreign minister and lead negotiator, Livni was closely involved in the talks with the Palestinian team, led by Ahmed Qurei. She was regarded as pragmatic and committed to a negotiated two-state settlement, but she also maintained firm positions on security and Israel’s identity as a Jewish state.

Rice’s discussions in Israel were expected to include the question of whether negotiations could survive a political transition. U.S. officials appeared eager to ensure continuity, arguing that the issues under negotiation were national interests rather than the project of any single Israeli leader.

Still, the prospect of an Israeli leadership change complicated the American timetable. If Olmert stepped aside, a Kadima leadership race, coalition bargaining or early elections could consume months. That would make it more difficult for the Bush administration to achieve its stated goal of a peace agreement before leaving office.

### U.S. Diplomatic Message

Throughout the trip, Rice’s message was one of urgency mixed with caution. She warned against allowing political distractions or violence to derail negotiations, but she also appeared to recognize the limits of U.S. influence. The United States could facilitate, pressure and propose ideas, but final decisions rested with Israeli and Palestinian leaders.

Rice emphasized that the alternative to negotiations would be continued instability and a loss of hope among ordinary Israelis and Palestinians. She argued that the creation of a Palestinian state remained essential not only for Palestinians but also for Israel’s long-term security and democratic future.

Her visit underscored the central contradiction facing the peace process: diplomatic engagement was continuing at a high level, but political conditions on both sides were fragile. Abbas needed tangible gains to show Palestinians that negotiations could deliver results. Israel’s government was distracted by scandal and possible leadership change. And the United States was running out of time before the end of the Bush administration.

For now, Rice insisted the process was still alive. But with settlement disputes unresolved, Gaza divided from the West Bank, and Israel’s leadership in flux, the path to a final agreement remained uncertain.

counterfactuals.output:
**Bush administration lowers expectations for Mideast peace deal**

*WASHINGTON (CNN) — 2008*

The Bush administration is increasingly backing away from President Bush’s once-stated goal of securing an Israeli-Palestinian peace agreement before he leaves office, even as Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice insists that U.S.-backed negotiations launched at Annapolis have moved both sides closer to the creation of a Palestinian state.

Administration officials now acknowledge privately and publicly that a final-status agreement by January is unlikely, citing persistent gaps between Israeli and Palestinian negotiators on borders, security, Jerusalem and the fate of Palestinian refugees. Political turmoil in Israel and divisions among Palestinians have further complicated the diplomatic push.

Still, Rice argued this week that the process begun at the November 2007 Annapolis conference has produced meaningful progress.

“We are laying the foundation for the establishment of a Palestinian state,” Rice said, emphasizing that Israelis and Palestinians have engaged in the most sustained direct negotiations in years. “This is hard work, but the work that has been done will endure.”

The Annapolis meeting brought Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert and Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas together under U.S. sponsorship, with Bush declaring at the time that a peace treaty was possible before the end of 2008. Since then, negotiators have met repeatedly, often away from cameras, in an effort to outline terms for a two-state solution.

But expectations have steadily diminished. Olmert’s political standing has been weakened by corruption investigations, while Abbas governs only the West Bank after Hamas seized control of Gaza in 2007. Israel has continued settlement activity that Palestinians say undermines confidence in the talks, while Israeli officials point to continuing security threats, including rocket fire from Gaza.

White House officials have begun describing the goal less as a completed peace treaty and more as leaving behind a negotiating framework for the next U.S. administration. Asked whether an agreement could still be reached before Bush leaves office, one senior official said the administration remains committed to “pushing as hard as possible,” but would not predict success.

Palestinian negotiators have expressed frustration that the talks have not produced visible changes on the ground, including a settlement freeze or a major easing of movement restrictions in the West Bank. Israeli officials, meanwhile, say any agreement must include strong guarantees that a future Palestinian state will not become a base for attacks.

Rice, who has made repeated trips to the region during Bush’s final year in office, has tried to keep the negotiations alive while defending the administration’s record.

“No one should underestimate how far the parties have come in discussing the core issues,” she said. “The United States believes there is now a clearer path toward Palestine than there was before Annapolis.”

Critics say the administration waited too long to make Israeli-Palestinian diplomacy a priority and is now running out of time. Supporters argue that Annapolis restarted a serious political process after years of violence and diplomatic stagnation.

Whether that process results in a final agreement remains doubtful. But Rice and other administration officials appear determined to portray it as an unfinished, but significant, step toward the long-promised goal of two states living side by side in peace.

**RAMALLAH, West Bank (CNN) —** U.S. Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice pressed Israeli and Palestinian leaders Monday to keep peace negotiations alive despite deep political uncertainty in Israel, saying she still believed an agreement outlining a future Palestinian state could be reached before President Bush leaves office.

Rice, on her eighth trip to the region since the U.S.-sponsored Annapolis peace conference last November, met Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas in Ramallah after talks with Israeli officials in Jerusalem. The Annapolis process set an ambitious goal of reaching a peace deal by the end of 2008.

“I continue to believe that it is possible to reach an agreement by the end of the year,” Rice said in Ramallah, standing alongside Abbas. “I know that the parties are working hard, and we are working hard with them.”

Rice said the United States was focused on helping both sides narrow gaps on the core issues that have long blocked a final settlement — borders, security, Jerusalem and the fate of Palestinian refugees.

“What is important is that this process continue,” she said. “The United States will remain very actively engaged.”

But the latest round of diplomacy comes as Israeli politics threaten to overshadow the negotiations. Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert has said he will resign after his Kadima Party chooses a new leader, following corruption investigations that have weakened his government and raised questions about whether he has the authority to make major concessions in peace talks.

Kadima’s leadership race could produce a new prime minister if the winner is able to form a governing coalition. If not, Israel could face early national elections — a process that could delay or even freeze substantive negotiations for months.

Palestinian officials have expressed concern that Olmert’s status as a lame-duck leader makes it harder to conclude a meaningful agreement. Israeli officials, meanwhile, say negotiations can continue, but any far-reaching deal would require political backing from a stable government.

The uncertainty complicates the Bush administration’s final push for a diplomatic achievement in the Middle East. Rice has traveled repeatedly to the region since Annapolis, trying to maintain momentum while also urging Israel to ease restrictions on Palestinian movement and pressing the Palestinians to strengthen security forces in the West Bank.

Abbas said the Palestinians remained committed to negotiations but emphasized that progress must be tangible.

“We want a comprehensive agreement that ends the occupation and leads to the establishment of an independent Palestinian state,” Abbas said.

Rice acknowledged the difficulties but warned against allowing political turbulence to derail the talks.

“There have been obstacles before, and there will be obstacles ahead,” she said. “But the only way to resolve this conflict is through negotiation.”

**WASHINGTON (AP-style) —** Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice expressed cautious optimism Wednesday that Israeli and Palestinian leaders could make meaningful progress toward a peace agreement following the U.S.-hosted Annapolis summit, even as the White House sought to temper expectations by saying a deal was unlikely before the end of the year.

Rice, who played a central role in bringing Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert and Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas together at the Maryland conference, said the renewed negotiations represented a serious opportunity to pursue a two-state solution. She emphasized that both sides had agreed to resume direct talks and to work toward resolving the core issues that have long divided Israelis and Palestinians, including borders, security, refugees and the status of Jerusalem.

Her upbeat assessment came after the Annapolis meeting, where the United States attempted to restart a peace process that had been largely stalled for years. The conference drew participation not only from Israel and the Palestinians, but also from a broad range of Arab states and international partners, giving the Bush administration what it described as a new opening for diplomacy in the Middle East.

Rice said the significance of Annapolis lay not in any immediate breakthrough, but in the fact that both parties had recommitted themselves publicly to negotiations aimed at creating an independent Palestinian state living alongside Israel in peace and security.

“This is the beginning of a process,” Rice said in substance, stressing that difficult work remained ahead. She argued that the political conditions were more favorable than they had been in years, with Abbas committed to negotiations and Olmert publicly backing the goal of a two-state settlement.

But White House press secretary Dana Perino offered a more restrained assessment, saying the administration did not expect an agreement to be completed before the end of the year. Perino’s comments underscored the gap between the diplomatic momentum the administration hoped to generate and the formidable obstacles facing negotiators.

The Bush administration has said it wants the two sides to reach a peace agreement before President George W. Bush leaves office, but officials have repeatedly acknowledged that the timetable is ambitious. Perino’s remarks appeared designed to prevent the Annapolis summit from being judged by whether it produced quick results.

The contrast between Rice’s optimism and Perino’s caution reflected the administration’s broader challenge: encouraging Israelis and Palestinians to take political risks while avoiding unrealistic expectations that could doom the process if early progress proves slow.

Israeli and Palestinian officials agreed at Annapolis to launch immediate bilateral talks and to meet regularly under U.S. supervision. The two sides also reaffirmed their commitment to the international “road map” peace plan, which calls for Israel to freeze settlement activity and for the Palestinians to strengthen security efforts and dismantle militant groups.

Those requirements remain among the most contentious elements of the process. Palestinian leaders have repeatedly demanded a halt to Israeli settlement construction in the West Bank and east Jerusalem, areas Palestinians seek for a future state. Israeli officials, meanwhile, have insisted that the Palestinian Authority must do more to prevent attacks and restore control, particularly after Hamas seized the Gaza Strip earlier in the year.

The split between Abbas’ West Bank-based government and Hamas-controlled Gaza further complicates the negotiations. Israel and the United States have refused to deal with Hamas unless it renounces violence, recognizes Israel and accepts previous agreements. Abbas has argued that a credible political process is essential to strengthening moderates and weakening extremists.

Rice has presented the renewed talks as part of a broader strategy to support moderate Arab and Palestinian forces at a time of deep regional instability. The administration also sees Arab participation in Annapolis as a sign that key U.S. allies in the region are prepared to support Israeli-Palestinian peacemaking, at least diplomatically.

Still, analysts and former negotiators have warned that previous rounds of talks collapsed over the same final-status issues now back on the table. The Clinton administration’s efforts at Camp David in 2000 failed to produce an agreement, and violence soon overtook the peace process during the second Palestinian uprising.

For Bush, Annapolis marked a late-term effort to make progress on an issue that had not been a sustained priority during much of his presidency, particularly after the Sept. 11 attacks and the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq. Rice, however, has increasingly devoted her diplomacy to the Israeli-Palestinian track, arguing that the conflict remains central to regional perceptions of U.S. policy.

Perino’s statement that a deal was unlikely before year’s end did not amount to a rejection of the administration’s broader goal. Rather, it signaled that the White House expected negotiations to unfold over months, not weeks. Officials said the immediate objective was to establish a durable framework for talks and keep both sides engaged.

Rice acknowledged that no one could guarantee success. But she maintained that the Annapolis summit had created a structure for serious negotiations and that the parties themselves had accepted responsibility for moving forward.

The coming weeks were expected to test whether the optimism surrounding Annapolis could survive the realities on the ground: Israeli settlement disputes, Palestinian security concerns, internal political opposition on both sides and continuing violence.

For now, the administration is trying to strike a delicate balance — presenting Annapolis as a meaningful diplomatic turning point while warning that the path to any final agreement remains uncertain and difficult.
